catalog_quote: There is some diachronic evidence for some English LOLIs integrating phonologically into LC with regards to vowel rounding and stress placement. English ‘Christmas’ surfaces in LC as [krismis] or [krismys], the presence of [y] in the latter form suggesting that the process of vowel rounding examined in §5.2 has started to act on that English LOLI. Morgan (1970) transcribes this word with penultimate stress, as in English: [ˈkrismis] cf. English /ˈkɹɪsməs/. In T2017 and M2017 corpora, however, this word occurs in all instances with stress on the final syllable as is typical in LC: [krisˈmis], [krisˈmys]. Based on this shift in stress and the presence of the front rounded vowel [y], it appears that this LOLI has been integrated over time via the adoption of LC phonological features. [p. 214] ... given the well-documented phonological similarities between the phonologies LC, LF and LE which include: vowel nasalization, glide reduction, th-stopping, unaspirated stops [p t k] and word-final stress (Carmichael 2013, in press; Dubois & Horvarth 1998, 2003a, 2003b, 2004; Oetting & Garrity 2006).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable of the word; English loans are integrated by shifting their stress to the final syllable (e.g. krisˈmis 'Christmas'). Stated in passing by a fieldworker, not in a dedicated stress section. The community orthography guide (Landry et al. 2016, p. 9) states the same rule: 'As a general rule, the final syllable in words.. are stressed.'
new_statements.exceptions: None in Mayeux 2019. Landry et al. 2016 (orthography guide) notes that acute-marked é /e/ 'does not follow this stressed pattern' and that some non-final syllables are stressed and marked with an acute; Morgan 1970 is reported to have transcribed the loan 'Christmas' with English-style penultimate stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ([krisˈmis] cited as a lexical item; 'word-final stress' p. 214). Mayeux 2019 p. 7177-7220 (§4) separately mentions sentence-level stress on the AAE-derived marker BIN, which is prosodic focus, not word stress. Language of Mayeux's 2017 corpora: Teche (T2017) and Mississippi/Pointe Coupee-area (M2017) varieties.
new_statements.identity_note: Mayeux 2019's statement is for contemporary Louisiana Creole generally, based on his 2017 Teche-region (T2017) and Mississippi/Pointe Coupee-area (M2017) corpora; the language-level glottocode loui1240 covers both. The major grammars describe single varieties: Klingler 2003 = Pointe Coupee, Neumann 1985 = Breaux Bridge (Teche), Morgan 1959 = St. Martin (Teche). Glottolog 5.1 has no separate dialect glottocodes for these under loui1240 in the record supplied.

sources.note: Ch. 5 'Phonology' (p. 189ff) covers only front-vowel rounding; but p. 213 (§6.4.1.2) states that in the author's 2017 corpora English loan 'Christmas' is 'in all instances' stressed 'on the final syllable as is typical in LC' ([krisˈmis]), contrasting with Morgan 1970's penultimate transcription; p. 214 lists 'word-final stress' among well-documented features shared by Louisiana Creole, Louisiana French and Louisiana English (citing Carmichael 2013, Dubois & Horvath).

sources.citation: Landry, Christophe, Cliford St. Laurent & Michael Gisclair (with contributions from Oliver F. Mayeux & Eric Gaither). 2016. Kouri-Vini: A Guide to Louisiana Creole Orthography. Louisiana Historic & Cultural Vistas, 17 pp.
sources.note: §2.2.1.1 'Stress', p. 9: 'Similar to Spanish, Louisiana Creole has stressed syllables. As a general rule, the final syllable in words–specifically words and names ending in the letter-A–are stressed. For this reason, we do not use the acute on final vowels. On all other syllables, however, which are less frequent, we do use the acute.' (community orthography guide, not a linguistic description).
